corpus_definition: A small round piece of medicine you swallow.

forms.definition: a small solid piece of medicine that you swallow whole
forms.example: She took a pill for her headache.

syn.note: Almost the same; tablet is common in British English and on medicine boxes.
A capsule is a pill with a soft or plastic outside that holds the medicine.
Medicine is the general word; it can also be a liquid or a cream.

forms.definition: (of wool or cloth) to become covered in very small balls
forms.example: My old sweater started to pill after a few washes.
forms.note: Belongs to pill = small balls on old clothes, not medicine. Mainly British; also called bobbling.
No adjective in this family.
No adverb in this family.

context.text: Dilnoza had a bad cold, so the doctor gave her some pills. She has to take one pill every morning after breakfast.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged. Compounds (pillbox) left out.

corpus_definition: A criminal who steals things from ships at sea.

forms.definition: a person who attacks ships at sea and steals from them
forms.example: The pirate looked for hidden gold on the island.

syn.note: An old word for a sea robber, used mostly in stories.
Any person who steals from people or places, not only at sea.
A general word for someone who steals, usually secretly.

forms.definition: the crime of attacking ships at sea and stealing from them
forms.example: Piracy is still a problem near some coasts.
forms.note: It also means illegally copying films, music or software.

syn.note: The crime of stealing, anywhere; piracy happens at sea.

forms.definition: to copy and sell films, music or software illegally
forms.example: Someone pirated the new film and put it online.
forms.note: Belongs to pirate = illegal copying, not robbers at sea.

forms.definition: copied and sold illegally, without paying the owner
forms.example: He bought a pirated DVD at the market.
forms.note: Belongs to pirate = illegal copying, not robbers at sea.
No adverb in this family.

context.text: In old stories, pirates sailed the seas and stole gold from other ships. Piracy still happens today, so some ships carry guards.

reviewer_note: Headword is itself a person noun, so it stays the main noun entry; the verb and pirated belong to the copying meaning.

corpus_definition: Deciding how to do something before you start.

forms.definition: the work of deciding how to do something before you start
forms.example: Careful planning made the event successful.

syn.note: Preparation also includes getting things ready, not only deciding.
Organization is about arranging people and things so they work well. British spelling: organisation.

ant.note: Doing something without preparing, deciding as you go.

forms.definition: an idea or arrangement for doing something in the future
forms.example: Our plan is to visit Bukhara in the summer.

syn.note: An idea is a thought; a plan has steps for doing it.
A big or official plan; in American English it can sound dishonest.
A plan for reaching a big goal over a long time.

forms.definition: to decide how you will do something before you do it
forms.example: We planned our trip to Samarkand very carefully.

syn.note: Organize also means arranging people and things. British spelling: organise.
Prepare means getting ready, often by doing things before an event.
Arrange is about fixing times and details with other people.

ant.note: To do something without preparing before.

forms.definition: decided or arranged before it happens
forms.example: The planned trip to the mountains was cancelled because of rain.

syn.note: A little more formal; what someone wants to happen.
Fixed for a certain time, like a train or a meeting.

ant.note: Not decided before; it just happened.
Done because you suddenly want to, without planning.

forms.note: No adverb in this family. Say 'as planned' or 'according to plan'.

people.definition: a person whose job is deciding how towns or events will be organized
people.example: The city planner wants more parks in Tashkent.
people.note: Also a book or app where you write your plans.

context.text: Aziz and his friends planned a surprise party for their teacher. The planning took two weeks, but the party went exactly as planned.

reviewer_note: Headword is the -ing noun; plan (noun and verb) is the root, so both are shown as forms. Unplanned kept as an opposite, not a form.

corpus_definition: A substance that causes illness or death if eaten.

forms.definition: a substance that can make you very ill or kill you
forms.example: Keep the poison away from children.

syn.note: A more scientific word, often for natural substances made by plants or animals.
The dangerous liquid from a snake or spider bite.

ant.note: A substance that stops a poison from hurting you.

forms.definition: to harm or kill someone by giving them a dangerous substance
forms.example: In the story, the evil queen tries to poison the princess.

syn.note: To make something dirty or dangerous, like water or food.
Used for air, water and land, not for people.

forms.definition: able to make you very ill or kill you if you eat or touch it
forms.example: Some mushrooms in the forest are poisonous.

syn.note: Very close; toxic is common for chemicals and gases.
Able to kill; stronger.
Causing damage, but not always serious.

forms.definition: with a dangerous substance put in it on purpose
forms.example: The detective found the poisoned cup of tea.

forms.note: No adverb in learner use.

people.definition: a person who harms or kills someone with a dangerous substance
people.example: The police finally caught the poisoner.

context.text: My grandmother keeps rat poison on a high shelf. She always tells us that some berries in the garden are poisonous, so we never eat them.

reviewer_note: Poisonous (naturally dangerous) vs poisoned (a dangerous substance was added); both kept.

corpus_definition: to rub a surface until it becomes smooth and shiny

forms.definition: a cream or liquid you rub on something to make it shine
forms.example: He put some black polish on his school shoes.

syn.note: A type of polish made from wax, used on floors, cars and furniture.
The bright look that comes after polishing: 'give your shoes a shine'.

forms.definition: to rub a surface until it becomes smooth and bright
forms.example: She spent the morning polishing the old wooden floor.

syn.note: Informal and easy: 'shine your shoes'.
To rub with a soft cloth to make it shine.
Rub is the general movement; you polish to make something shiny.

ant.note: When metal becomes dark and loses its shine.

forms.definition: smooth and shiny because someone has rubbed it
forms.example: The polished table looked like new.
forms.note: It can also mean done with great skill: a polished performance.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word.
Smooth and shiny, often used for paper, hair and paint.

ant.note: Not rubbed to make it shine.

forms.note: No adverb in this family.

people.definition: a machine or tool used to make floors or cars shine
people.example: The cleaner used an electric polisher on the hall floor.

context.text: Before the wedding, Bobur polished his shoes with black polish. Now they are so polished that he can see his face in them.

reviewer_note: Trap: Polish with a capital P (from Poland) is a different word with a different sound; not part of this family.

corpus_definition: the activities related to how a country is governed.

forms.definition: the activities and ideas connected with how a country is governed
forms.example: She enjoys reading about modern politics.
forms.note: Takes a singular verb: 'Politics is interesting.'

syn.note: The group of people who run a country, or the act of running it.
A formal phrase for the questions and events that matter to a whole country.

forms.definition: to make a question or event a matter of party arguments
forms.example: Some people politicize every discussion about the city's water.
forms.note: British spelling: politicise.

forms.definition: connected with government and the way a country is run
forms.example: There are three political parties in the election.

syn.note: Connected with the government itself, not with parties or ideas.
Connected with a city or with the duties of citizens.

ant.note: Not interested in or not connected with party ideas.

forms.definition: in a way that is connected with government and parties
forms.example: The country is politically stable.

people.definition: a person who works in government or wants to be elected
people.example: The politician promised to build new schools.

context.text: My father watches the news every evening because he is interested in politics. He likes to talk about political ideas with his friends at the choyxona.

reviewer_note: Politics takes a singular verb; politic (wise) and policy left out as different words for learners.

corpus_definition: Dirty or harmful substances in the air or water.

forms.definition: dirty or harmful substances in the air, water or land
forms.example: Factory smoke causes a lot of pollution.

syn.note: More formal and often about one place or thing, like water or food.
Dirt is any dust or mud; pollution is harmful and often made by people.

forms.definition: to make air, water or land dirty and harmful
forms.example: Old cars pollute the air in big cities.

syn.note: Very close; a little more formal.
Stronger: to make something deadly.
Easy word; to make something not clean.

ant.note: To make water or air completely clean.

forms.definition: made dirty and harmful by chemicals, smoke or rubbish
forms.example: Nobody swims in the polluted river anymore.

syn.note: Very close; often used for water, food or ground.
Easy, everyday word.

ant.note: Not made dirty; still natural and clean.

forms.note: No adverb in this family.

people.definition: a substance that makes air, water or land dirty
people.example: Plastic is one of the worst pollutants in the sea.

people.definition: a person, company or country that makes the environment dirty
people.example: The government wants big polluters to pay more.

context.text: Many cars and factories pollute the air in Tashkent in winter. Some days the pollution is so bad that people wear masks in the polluted streets.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged. Pollutant (the substance) and polluter (who does it) kept in People & things, not the noun slot.

corpus_definition: To make a short, sharp sound like a small explosion.

forms.definition: a short, sharp sound like a small explosion
forms.example: We heard a loud pop when the balloon burst.

syn.note: A bang is usually louder.
A sharp sound like wood or a whip breaking.

forms.definition: to burst or open with a short, sharp sound
forms.example: The balloon will pop if you touch it.
forms.note: Informally it also means to go somewhere quickly: 'I'll pop into the shop.'

syn.note: Burst is about breaking open; it does not always make a sound.
To make a loud, sudden noise.
To make a sharp sound, often when something breaks.

forms.note: No adjective in this family. Pop in 'pop music' or 'a pop star' comes from popular, a different word.
No adverb in learner use. People say 'go pop': 'The balloon went pop.'

context.text: Laylo was making popcorn in the kitchen. The corn started to pop, and every few seconds we heard another loud pop.

reviewer_note: Trap: pop music and pop (fizzy drink) are different words, not this sound family; compound popcorn left out of forms.

corpus_definition: The specific role or job that you hold.

forms.definition: a job in a company or organization
forms.example: He applied for a position as manager.

syn.note: Everyday word; position is more formal and used in job adverts.
Formal, mainly British: 'She was offered the post of director.'
What you do in a team or company, not only the job title.
A job that is empty and waiting for someone.

forms.definition: to put someone or something in a particular place
forms.example: She positioned the chairs around the table.
forms.note: Belongs to position = a place, not a job.
No adjective in learner use for the job meaning. Positive is a different word.
No adverb in this family.

context.text: My sister has a new position at a bank in Tashkent. It is a good position, and she hopes to become a manager next year.

reviewer_note: Kept to the job meaning; the verb belongs to the place meaning. Positive is not family. No affix claimed (posit + -ion is not a learner split).

corpus_definition: useful and effective in a real situation

forms.definition: how useful and sensible something is in real life
forms.example: When buying a car, my father thinks first about practicality.

syn.note: Easy word; about being helpful.
Being easy to use and saving time.

forms.definition: real action and doing, not just ideas
forms.example: The idea sounds good, but will it work in practice?
forms.note: Also means doing something again and again to improve: piano practice.

syn.note: Doing things, not only thinking.
What is true in real life.

ant.note: Ideas about how something should work, not real action.

forms.definition: to do something again and again to get better at it
forms.example: I practise my English every day with an app.
forms.note: Belongs to practice = training, not being useful. British spelling; American English uses practice for the verb too.

forms.definition: useful and sensible in a real situation
forms.example: A warm coat is a practical choice for cold weather.

syn.note: Easy word; helps you do something.
Showing good judgement, not silly.
Made to be used, not just to look nice.
Informal: useful and easy to use.

ant.note: Not useful or sensible in real life.

forms.definition: in a useful and sensible way in real life
forms.example: She dresses practically for her long walk to work.
forms.note: Careful: practically most often means 'almost': 'The bus was practically empty.'

syn.note: In a way that shows good judgement.

ant.note: In ideas, not in real life.

people.definition: a person who works in a skilled job, such as a doctor
people.example: She went to see a medical practitioner about her back.
people.note: Belongs to practice = the work of a doctor or lawyer, not being useful.

context.text: My mother always gives practical advice. Her ideas sound simple, but they work well in practice, so the whole family listens to her.

reviewer_note: False-friend trap: practically usually means 'almost'; kept as existing with a clear note. Impractical is an opposite, not a form.
